I.          Introduction

[
1
]

Nicholas Chan was found guilty on 20 July 2004 of selling 56 g of heroin
for $7,000 and possession of that $7,000 as property obtained by crime. The
facts that gave rise to these convictions are set out in the Reasons for
Judgment of the Trial judge, Justice John Moore:
2004 ABQB 560
. They include
Chan’s representation about the heroin (it turned out to be 71% pure) and his
knowledge of its availability:

Yes, he told me it was the best.
That there was only, I believe, two or three sources for No. 4 in the Calgary
area.

[
2
]

Moore J. recused himself from sentencing Chan on 20 December 2004 for
reasons described at
[2004] A.J. No. 1616
. He refused an application for a
mistrial but set the question of sentencing to another judge pursuant to
s.
669.2
of the
Criminal Code
.

[
3
]

I first characterize Chan’s crime of trafficking. Trafficking in heroin
can range from a gift from one addict to another of a sufficient amount for a
single ingestion to multi-kilogram international trafficking. For the latter,
see
R v. Richa
(1974),
1974 CanLII 1558 (ON CA)
, 18 C.C.C. (2d) 63 (Ont. C.A.). Richa was
considered to be operating on an executive level in the organization to which
he belonged and was sentenced to life imprisonment.

[
4
]

Counsel for Chan suggests that I characterize this as low-level
trafficking on more than a minimal scale, which would attract a starting point
of five years, leaving aside mitigating and aggravating features. The Crown’s
position is that this is more akin to wholesale trafficking and that the
correct starting point sentence is 7½ to 8 years.

[
5
]

In Alberta the most recent appellate cases dealing with trafficking in
heroin are
R. v. Phun
(1997), 120 C.C.C. (3d) 550 (Alta. C.A.),
and
R. v. Ostertag
(2000), 35 C.R. (5th) 350,
2000 ABCA 232
. In
Phun
,
the Court held that the appropriate range for lower level commercial
trafficking in heroin on more than a minimal scale is five years (para. 35).
Phun

had sold 1 g of 95% pure heroin for $550 and had said he could deliver more,
although he did not do so. At para. 19, the Court cited
R. v. Lang
,

[1978] A.J. No. 281 (C.A.)
, where trafficking two caps of heroin and possession
of 12 g of heroin having a street value of $8,500 resulted in an increase in
sentence to six years concurrent. In
Ostertag
, the Court held
that Ostertag, an addict who had sold 1.9 g of heroin for $1,000, should get
the benefit of a late guilty plea, time spent in custody and a willingness to
become involved in rehabilitation programs to result in a sentence of four
years.

[
6
]

In my view, the sale of 56 g of heroin for $7,000 when Chan is not
addict, and given his knowledge of the heroin market in Calgary (referred to
above), compels characterization of Chan as an intermediate or mid-level
participant in wholesale trafficking. With a starting point of five years for
lower level trafficking, intermediate level trafficking should therefore
attract a sentence of 7½ years with executive level trafficking attracting
10 years plus.

[
7
]

Having made this characterization, I will not use it as an aggravating
feature. I do not consider Chan’s criminal record to be an aggravating feature
as it is minor and unconnected to these crimes. As for mitigating features, I
take into account his relative youth (he is 27) and the support of his mother
and his sister. I do not see much evidence of work or further education after
high school, but I do not consider this to be an aggravating feature but rather
consider it to be something to take into account in assessing Chan’s prospects
for rehabilitation. General and specific deterrence are the primary objectives.
Apart from the
Charter
arguments and the credit‑for-time
arguments, the appropriate sentence for Chan’s conviction for trafficking in
heroin would be 7½ years’ imprisonment.

II.        Nature
of Chan’s Application

A.        Procedural
History

[
8
]

The average stay in custody for a remand prisoner is 14 days. Chan has
been a remand prisoner since 12 June 2003, 26 months and one day. As mentioned,
Chan was convicted on 20 July 2004 of these charges. Thus the period of
incarceration from 12 June 2003 to 20 July 2004 can be classified as
pre-trial custody, while the time since 20 July 2004 relates to custody after
conviction but before sentence. The conditions of his stay in remand have led
him to seek remedies pursuant to the
Charter
. If he is not
successful in obtaining
Charter
relief, he asks for extraordinary
credit for the time that he has spent in remand in calculating his sentence. He
does not complain about the length of his stay in remand.

[
9
]

In a jurisdiction where an accused in custody can go to trial at the
Court of Queen’s Bench within six months, this case has taken a long time to
come to conclusion. The offences alleged in the indictment occurred 15 November
1999. It was alleged, and now has been proven, that Chan sold 56 g of heroin to
an undercover agent for $7,000. A warrant was issued for his arrest on 27 June
2000 and he was arrested on 20 September 2000. He was released from custody the
next day on his own recognizance with a $1,500 cash deposit. The first day of
evidence of the preliminary inquiry occurred 5 December 2000. The second day of
the preliminary inquiry was  April 2001, at which time Chan and two co‑accused
were committed to stand trial. Chan appeared at arraignments on 9 May 2001 and
the matter was set over to 13 June 2001, when a five‑day trial was set to
proceed 7 January 2002 (six months later). A pre-trial conference was set for 7
December 2001. At that conference, Chan’s first counsel, Jack Kelly, advised
that he had been discharged by Chan. Therefore, the January trial date was
vacated and the case was remanded to arraignments on 9 January 2002. On 9
January 2002 a new trial date was set for 16 September 2002. On that date,
Chan’s co‑accused (and brother), Timothy Chan, entered a guilty plea and
the matter was adjourned to 30 October 2002, at which time his guilty plea was
rejected. The matter was set over to arraignments in December 2002. In December
2002 a trial date was set for 8 September 2003.

[
10
]

[
11
]

On 2 September 2003 Patrick Fagan, new counsel for Chan, applied for an
adjournment of the trial set for 8 September 2003. The new trial date set was
13 April 2004. On 29 October 2003 Chan’s bail was revoked on the
charges before this Court.

[
12
]

On 13 April 2004 the trial started. After three days it was adjourned to
13 May 2004 for two days of trial time and then to 23 June 2004 for two more
days. It was then set over to 20 July 2004, at which time Moore J.
convicted Chan. Sentencing was adjourned to 20 August 2004 at Fagan’s
request. On 20 August 2004 the sentencing hearing was again adjourned to 27
September 2004 at Fagan’s request. On that date, it was adjourned once more to
19 October 2004 at Fagan’s request, and then once more to 28 October 2004. Chan
then dismissed Fagan as counsel and new counsel Tom Engel began representing
Chan. He filed a motion relating to
Charter
breaches arising from
Chan’s incarceration.

[
13
]

On 1 December 2004 the sentencing hearing commenced. The hearing was
interrupted and adjourned to the next day. On 2 December 2004 Engel applied for
a mistrial which application was set to 20 December 2004. Time was also set in
the new year for the continuation of the sentencing procedure in the weeks of 7
February and 3 March 2005. On 20 December 2004 Moore J. dismissed the
application for mistrial but held that he would not continue as the Trial judge
pursuant to
s. 669.2
of the
Criminal Code
.

B.
R.
v. Weaver

[
14
]

On 4 April 2005 the hearing commenced before me. Ten days were available
for Chan’s case. One of the preliminary questions before me was the application
of the
Charter
. Moore J. had previously ruled that
Charter

relief was not available to Chan. On 10 March 2005 the Alberta Court of Appeal
released its decision in
R. v. Weaver
(2005), 194 C.C.C. (3d)
350,
2005 ABCA 105
. In
Weaver
, the learned Provincial Court Judge
found that the accused had been arbitrarily detained in violation of his rights
under s. 9 of the
Charter
and granted a judicial stay of
proceedings. The accused had been kept in jail overnight after his arrest
because he was too intoxicated to be released. He should have been released at
7:00 a.m. but was not released until 10:00 a.m. The Provincial Court Judge
found, on the basis of
R. v. Cutforth
(1987),
1987 CanLII 114 (AB CA)
, 40 C.C.C. (3d) 253
(Alta. C.A.), that no exclusionary remedy was available to him, that is to say
that he could not exclude the proof of service of the certificate of analysis;
so, on the theory that if there is a
Charter
breach there must be
a remedy, the remedy he granted was a judicial stay of proceedings. The Crown’s
appeal to the Court of Queen’s Bench was unsuccessful. At the Court of Appeal,
the majority held that the Supreme Court of Canada decision in
R. v.
Simpson
,
1995 CanLII 120 (SCC)
, [1995] 1 S.C.R. 449, had overruled
Cutforth

insofar as
Cutforth
is authority for the proposition that the
Charter

breach must be clearly exploratory of the issues raised by the indictment or
information being tried. In other words, even if the breach does not give rise
to a defence in law or create evidence that should be excluded, under s. 24(1)
a court may grant a stay or other
Charter
remedy citing,
inter
alia
,
R. v. Pringle
(2003),
2003 ABPC 7 (CanLII)
, 324 A.R. 352 at 379 (Prov. Ct.).
At para. 19 of
Weaver
, the majority stated:

It follows that jurisdiction over
the subject matter includes
Charter
breaches that arise in the context
of the State’s investigation and detention of accused persons. The infringement
need not be exploratory of the issues raised by the indictment, or Information,
being tried. Nor need the infringement give rise to the exclusion of evidence
under s. 24(2) of the
Charter
.

[
15
]

McFadyen J.A. concurred in the result.

[
16
]

The majority therefore held that the learned Provincial Court Judge
erred in holding that there must be a strict causal link between the arbitrary
detention and the evidence in order to exclude the evidence and, as well, the
Provincial Court Judge erred (although it was not argued before him) in failing
to distinguish
Cutforth
on the basis that evidence of service of
the certificate of analysis could have been excluded because there was a
temporal nexus between the arbitrary detention and service. In addition, the
majority held that the Provincial Court Judge erred in equating a clear breach
of the
Charter
with a clear case for a stay, for the Supreme
Court of Canada in
R. v. O’Connor
,
1995 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 411, had ruled
that a stay of proceedings is “a
last resort
, to be taken when all other
acceptable avenues of protecting the accused’s right to full answer and defence
are exhausted” (para. 77) (emphasis in original), or “where irreparable
prejudice would be caused to the integrity of the judicial system if the
prosecution were continued” (para. 82). The majority held that both the
Provincial Court Judge and the Court of Queen’s Bench Judge had failed to
consider the guideline cases, including
O’Connor
,
before
granting a stay. Therefore, the matter was sent back for a new trial.

[
17
]

Counsel agreed before me, and I have acted on the basis, that a stay in
respect of the sentence of Chan is an available remedy for a
Charter

breach. Counsel for Chan also says that a reduction in sentence is another
Charter

remedy available. I must say in passing that the admonition of McClung J.A. in
Cutforth

that trials would bloat were
Charter
remedies available for
matters unrelated to the investigation of a case or the production of evidence
seems apt. I have heard 17 days of testimony. There is now 2,988 pages of
transcript. However, it is settled law in Alberta that evidence must be led to
justify more than the usual two‑for‑one credit for time spent in
custody prior to sentencing. See, e.g.,
R.v. Roberts
,
2005 ABCA
11
at para.
72
, and
R. v. La
, [2003] 8 W.W.R. 94,
2003 ABQB 391
.
Thus, the evidence that has been developed in great detail is not solely or
necessarily attributable to the development of facts that would support
Charter

arguments, for the facts developed also bear on the difficulties of pre‑sentence
custody in relation to its direct effects on Chan and the issue of whether
extraordinary credit should be granted in consequence.

D.        Description
of Calgary and Red Deer Physical Remand Facilities

[
20
]

Given Engel’s submission that the treatment and conditions afforded Chan
while in remand were exceptionally harsh, it will be useful to describe the
physical layout of the remand centres where he spent most of his time. These
details will be important when considering the evidence. Except for nine days
in Edmonton and seven days in Peace River, since 12 June 2003 Chan has been in
custody in either the Calgary Remand Centre (CRC) or the Red Deer Remand Centre
(RDRC). Other than some disagreement about average cell size, all the witnesses
described the physical aspects of the two centres in a similar fashion.

1.         CRC

[
21
]

The CRC was built in 1993 and designed for a capacity of 468 inmates.
The average population over the last 18 months has been 510-515 inmates. There
are 14 units in the CRC, including a number of medium security units, which are
labelled the “general population”, maximum security, a female unit,
disciplinary segregation, a suicide watch unit and administrative segregation.
Up to eight inmates can be housed in administrative segregation. They are
placed there either because prison authorities believe they do not function
well in the general population or because they require protection. When
double-bunking occurs it is usually in the general population. The average stay
has been 14 days, but it is estimated that 15 to 20% of inmates stay for one
year and 5% stay for two years or longer.

[
22
]

Physical facilities at the CRC include an exercise yard, consisting of a
space 15 to 20 feet wide and 30 feet long. The yard has a concrete floor and
walls with a meshed open ceiling. The meshed ceiling prevents items from coming
into the centre. There is a gymnasium, a weight pit area and a book shelf
containing books which inmates can borrow. The common area consists of phones,
chairs and tables bolted to the floor as well as a 14-inch black-and-white
television. Located on site is a multi-faith chapel. Visitor facilities consist
of a visiting room with a pane of glass separating inmates from visitors and
requiring that phones be used for conversations.

[
23
]

Inmates in the general population can use these facilities on a rotating
basis. In the maximum security unit, inmates are allowed out for five hours one
day and six the next and at those times have access to a common area and an
outside yard. Administrative segregation inmates have only up to one hour per
day out of their cells. They are usually not able to use the gymnasium and
weight pit although they can use most of the other facilities. Disciplinary
segregation inmates are denied access to all common facilities and privileges
other than contact with their lawyers.

[
24
]

Chan estimates that the typical cell in Calgary is either 6 x 10 or 12
feet, while Kim Canning, the Deputy Director of Administration and Finance at
the CRC, estimates measurements to be 8 x 10 feet. While it is surprising that
neither party actually measured a cell, since the burden of proof is with Chan
I am prepared to accept the 8 x 10 measurement. Regardless of the exact
measurement, there is no question it is a small space for an inmate to be
confined for 23 hours or more per day. There is a window in the cell which
cannot be opened. Air is filtered through a vent system with air drawn from the
outside. Cells other than disciplinary segregation have a radio with five or
six pre-programmed stations, and inmates eat in their cells.

2.         RDRC

[
25
]

The RDRC was built in 1987 and has 64 general population beds and 40
beds for protective custody. The protective custody beds serve all of Alberta.
A limited number of local sentenced offenders are imprisoned at the RDRC.
Sentenced offenders work in the laundry or kitchen area. The average numbers in
the general population are 55-60, with 14 days being the average stay.
Overcrowding has not been an issue.

[
26
]

General population inmates eat their meals outside their cells. They may
be out of their cells 12 hours and 45 minutes per day on weekdays and 10 hours
and 30 minutes on weekends. All inmates are generally classified as maximum
security, although general population inmates are classified as minimum and
maximum security inmates within the facility. The common area facilities are
similar to the CRC’s, with an exercise yard, gymnasium, weight pit and mobile
library. Inmates have access to three pre-programmed radio stations in their
cells. Due to staffing limitations, general population inmates are able to use
the gymnasium only once per week.

[
27
]

A six-bed unit is utilized for administrative and disciplinary
segregation. All of these cells have a single bunk and inmates are normally
allowed out of their cells one hour per day, although this varies depending on
staffing levels. Segregation inmates have access to the yard and books but not
the gymnasium, weight pit or black-and-white television.

[
28
]

Chan describes the cell size in Red Deer as being similar to Calgary.
Gary McNaughton, the Director of the RDRC, estimates a typical cell size as
being 10 x 14 feet, with each cell built to house two inmates and having a
window with a view outdoors. McNaughton was a credible witness, and I accept
his estimated measurements.

E.         Chan’s
Remand Placement History

[
29
]

Chan has been in custody since 12 June 2003, 26 months and one day.
While there was some dispute about the number of days he spent in segregation,
I accept that the Crown’s calendar (Exhibit S-46) is accurate. Chan was not a
good historian. Statistics were provided from 13 June 2003 until 26 June 2005. Chan’s
history of placement can be broken down in the following way: He was imprisoned
in the general population for 191 days in Calgary, 307 days in Red Deer, 9 days
in Edmonton and 7 days in Peace River, for a total of 514 days. In terms of
administrative segregation, he was imprisoned for 129 days in Unit 9 in Calgary
and 75 days in Red Deer, for a total of 204 days. Disciplinary segregation time
was 16 days in Red Deer. Other Calgary placements were 9 days in administrative
segregation (ATU), 4 days in administrative segregation (Unit 8) and 3 days in
observation overflow (Unit 8), for a total of 16 days. There is some double
counting (11 days) that I assume arises from transfers between institutions.

[
30
]

These numbers show that while Chan has spent the majority of his time in
the general population, he has been subject to a significant period of
incarceration in administrative segregation. During this time, other than for
Court appearances, he was allowed out of his cell for only one hour or less per
day.

F.         Evidence
in Support of Complaints and Findings

[
31
]

Defence submissions include over 400 requests for interview forms which
Chan completed while in remand, all of which can be categorized as requests or
complaints, as well as other remand documents. There is also a psychologist’s
report, an engineer’s report regarding the safety of prison transport vans and
detailed testimony from Chan about the conditions he experienced. There is also
testimony from several other witnesses with knowledge of either correctional
centres or Chan’s experiences in remand centres. Other than some confusion over
dates and numbers, I found Chan to be a credible witness. A number of his
allegations were either not dealt with by the Crown or in fact confirmed by
Crown witnesses.

[
32
]

In my findings I specify whether I am giving credence to the complaints
as categorized such that the treatment or conditions complained about goes or
go beyond what has come to be termed as “hard time” in remand. Note that a
Charter

breach does not result just because treatment is or conditions are found to go
beyond hard time. This will be dealt with in the
Charter
section.
The summary of evidence and my findings are as follows:

1.         Cell
Effects/Searches

[
33
]

Chan’s primary complaint is that items he purchased from the remand
canteen were sometimes damaged during searches of his cell at the CRC. He also
objects to his personal property being removed from his cell and put in his
remand locker. He considers the CRC cell searches to be more damaging to his
property than cell searches at other remand centres. On cross-examination, Chan
said he did not think five garbage bags of property was a substantial amount
for a small cell. Chan agreed that in 2002 he was disciplined when remand
officials found a razor blade in his cell. At the time he had a cellmate and he
said he had no idea how the razor blade got there.

[
34
]

Luciano Bentenuto, an expert witness on security in the federal
correctional system, testified that, in the federal correctional system,
contraband has been found hidden in inmates’

personal items, including a shampoo bottle.

[
35
]

I accept the explanation of remand officials that Chan was accumulating
too much property in his cell, which was a fire hazard. As far as damage to his
canteen items, I view this as insignificant in context. I accept that officials
are required to search a cell thoroughly and that items may be damaged in
consequence. I am therefore giving no credence to this complaint.

2.         Strip
Searches

[
36
]

Chan says he finds strip searches to be degrading and dehumanizing and
that he feels violated by them. Leslie Block, a Chartered Psychologist,
testified Chan described to him the horror of being strip searched, which was
corroborated by testing. Chan described a typical strip search as starting with
a request to remove his clothes and turn around. Next he has been asked to lift
his arms and open his mouth and run his own fingers through his teeth. Normally
he has been asked to bend over slightly and then spread his buttock cheeks and
lift his scrotum. He said it depends on the guard and the remand centre whether
they insist he spread his buttock cheeks; some just let him bend down to pick
up his clothes. He has refused officers’ requests to put his fingers in his
mouth, spread his buttock cheeks and lift his scrotum because he thinks they
can do a thorough check without having these things done. He said he would not
put his fingers in his mouth because they are dirty and he has not had a chance
to wash them. He said there is no soap in the Arrival and Departure area where
the searches often take place.

[
37
]

Chan’s other complaint about strip searches is that they sometimes took
place in the view of other inmates. In Calgary there was a weekly clothing
exchange where three inmates at a time were forced to walk naked down a hall in
front of other inmates in order to receive clean clothes.

[
38
]

In response to these complaints, Kim Canning, the Deputy Director of
Administration and Finance at the CRC, testified that regular strip searches
are necessary for the protection of the inmates and remand officials. This
includes requiring inmates to spread their buttock cheeks and lift their
scrotums. He said drugs and weapons have been discovered during strip searches.

[
39
]

Bentenuto testified that similar methods are used for strip searches in
the federal system. He testified that inmates will sometimes intrude razor
blades in their orifices. He indicated that other methods of searching are not
effective. A metal detector for instance only picks up weapons that are metal.
An ion scanner would be effective to search for drugs but not weapons.

[
40
]

In addition to testimony from correctional officers on this point, in a
Fatality
Inquiries Act
Report dated 23 June 2003 into the death of an inmate by
overdose at the CRC (S-96), Provincial Court Judge Skene stated at para. 3: “It
was ridiculously easy for Mr. McLeod to obtain drugs while in custody.” The
drugs had been smuggled in someone’s rectum.

[
41
]

In response to the clothing exchange concern, Keith Bush, a correctional
officer in Calgary, testified that during the clothing exchange inmates are
naked and they walk 15 to 20 feet down the hall to exchange their clothes. He
said that he does not consider this to be a strip search but agreed that the
bodies of the inmates were inspected for signs of contraband. The Solicitor
General’s response to the Human Rights Commission regarding the clothing
exchange was that inmates exchange clean clothing three inmates at a time and
are not strip searched.

[
42
]

Dealing first with the issue of the clothing exchange, I accept that
this was a strip search since the inmates’ bodies were inspected. The
Correctional
Institution Regulation
, Alta. Reg. 205/2001, provides broad authority
in
s. 10
for strip searches in a correctional institution.
Section 10(3)

states that “searches of inmates are to be carried out in a manner so as to
respect the dignity of the inmate as far as possible without interfering with
the thoroughness of the search.” In my view, the clothing exchange does not
violate this provision.

[
43
]

I accept that Chan has been sincerely distressed by the strip searches.
However, thorough strip searches are an unpleasant necessity in a correctional
institution. The fact that guards at the RDRC did not always require Chan to
spread his buttock cheeks and lift his scrotum does not mean that the CRC
should be forced to follow the same approach. There is evidence that inmates
sometimes smuggle contraband in their orifices. Chan cannot be exempt from a
full strip search. To exempt him or others would put correctional staff, other
prisoners and himself at risk. Chan could smuggle drugs, or a weapon, knowing
he would not be searched thoroughly. Alternatively, other prisoners could
pressure Chan to carry items for them. That pressure could be applied directly
to Chan, or indirectly, by telling him his family could be harmed. There is
undoubtedly a legitimate and pressing need that prisoners be thoroughly
searched.

[
44
]

In the result, I give no credence to Chan’s complaints about strip
searches. His complaints about excessive force during strip searches will be
dealt with under the heading “Excessive Force/Lockup”.

3.         Denial
of Communication with Counsel

[
45
]

Chan complains that there were a limited number of phones available for
inmates. This was particularly difficult for him during his segregation time
because of the limited amount of time he had outside his cell. He testified
that the phones were right next to each other so there was no privacy when he
was phoning his lawyer. He also complained at length about a new remand phone
system in 2004 making all local calls by inmates collect calls and not allowing
calls out to various phone numbers including at one point his lawyer’s cell
phone.

[
46
]

Prison officials testified that the new phone system was taken out after
Court action in Edmonton. See
Criminal Trial Lawyers’ Assn. v. Alberta
(Solicitor General)
(2004), 188 C.C.C. (3d) 538,
2004 ABQB 534
. Canning
testified that they try to rotate the time inmates are out of their cells in
order to accommodate calls to lawyers. Lawyers can also visit inmates at the
institution.

[
47
]

While Chan’s complaints about the phone system have some merit, there is
no evidence that either he or one of his lawyers was unable to communicate on
any point of importance. I therefore do not accept that he was denied
communication with counsel and do not give credence to this complaint.

4.         Access
to Disclosure/Defence Material

[
48
]

There was little evidence about this complaint other than the allegation
that disclosure documents from Chan’s lawyers were among items confiscated when
items from his cell were put in storage. I accept the explanation from Canning
that there can be a problem with leaving disclosure material in inmates’ cells.
Other inmates may find this material, for example, disclosure about an alleged
sexual offence, and use it against that inmate. Further, other prisoners are
known to demand disclosure documents as a kind of “passport”, which I understand
allows prisoners to classify other prisoners according to jail house hierarchy.
Thus, I am giving no credence to this complaint.

5.         Religious
Diet

[
49
]

Chan described his religious beliefs as a combination of Buddhism,
Chinese Taoism and Confucianism. These are beliefs with which he was raised at
home. There is a vegetarian aspect of his faith, although he agreed that a
vegetarian diet was not always practised in his home. At the time he was first
incarcerated in October 2001 he described his diet as vegetarian, although he
ate a minimal amount of meat. When he was released in 2002 he continued to eat
vegetarian. He said he did eat meat in 2001 while in remand because he was “put
in that position”, but he testified that when he was re-admitted in 2003 he
made a decision not to let himself be coerced into eating meat.

[
50
]

Susie Li, a Buddhist monk who met Chan several times in the RDRC,
testified that she does not see any harm in believing in Buddhism, Chinese
Taoism and Confucianism. She said that, at the first level of spirituality, a
beginning practitioner such as Chan is asked to eat vegetarian to enhance his
compassion. She thought Chan knew very little about Buddhism when she met him
at the RDRC other than a little bit of two chants.

[
51
]

Chan requested a vegetarian meal for religious reasons on 5 January
2004. His request was denied by the CRC because the remand records listed his
religion as “none”. Chan admitted that when he was first admitted to remand in
2001 he answered “none” to the religious question because he did not think it
was any of their business. He said when he was admitted in 2003 he does not
recall being asked about his religion.

[
52
]

He made a follow-up request for a vegetarian meal also on 5 January 2004
asking for a chance to explain in person. His request was denied by Canning.
The reason recorded on the reply form was that “[w]e do not recognize
proselytism (conversion) during incarceration”. Proselytism and conversion are
two different things, a distinction now recognized by Canning.

[
53
]

A medical chart entry from a nurse on 22 January 2004 stated: “Requests
vegetarian diet in addition to no milk. Advised to speak with doctor.” Chan
said when he spoke several times with Dr. Gillespie the doctor told him a
vegetarian diet was not his concern because it was for religious reasons.

[
54
]

Chan testified that, except for the occasional mistake, while he was in
the RDRC they were complying with his request for a vegetarian diet. However he
said on 5 February 2004 there was a directive by the CRC to cancel his
vegetarian food in the RDRC and shortly afterwards the RDRC cancelled his
vegetarian diet. At this point Chan said he ate only the non-meat products on
his tray or sometimes nothing at all.

[
55
]

On 20 February 2004 at the CRC, he wrote on a request for interview form
that he was not getting adequate nutrition.

[
56
]

On 23 February 2004 at the CRC, in his request for interview form he
asked to see the Chaplain to discuss his diet. The response he received was:
“As your request for a vegetarian diet has nothing to do with religious
reasons, the chaplain cannot help you in this matter.”

[
57
]

On 18 March 2004 Chan met with Father Blanch, a Chaplain at the RDRC.
Father Blanch wrote a note stating:

Nicholas Chan has been a
vegetarian all his adult life. His mother and grandmother are practising
[Buddhists] and he feels drawn to their religious practise of a meat-free diet.

Nicholas is sincere in his
request for a meat-free diet and I recommend strongly that his request be
granted.

Chan said that after this note was written he did not get a
vegetarian meal right away but that the RDRC was trying to sort out the
situation with the CRC. In the meantime the RDRC gave him an extra peanut butter
sandwich.

[
58
]

While he was in the CRC he said he was on a hunger strike. A note of 8
April 2004 on the nurse’s chart stated that “inmate to be charged as per DDO
and placed in baby-dolls”.

[
59
]

There was an oral order of 13 April 2004 from Moore J. that Chan be
given vegetarian food but Chan said it was not followed for some time. He said
the CRC advised him they needed a copy of the order. On 14 April 2004 at the
CRC, in response to a request for interview form he completed requesting a
vegetarian meal, the reply was:

We do not have the order from the
judge yet. There is provision to change your religion by having someone in
authority from your religion interview you and confirm with us that you are a
practicing member of the religion. Please do so.

[
60
]

Chan said he mentioned Father Blanch’s note to a nurse at the CRC but
she responded that it was not her decision to issue a vegetarian diet. I agree,
by the way, with the Crown’s submission on this point that Chan’s counsel
should have prepared a written order, filed with the Court, and served it on
the CRC.

[
61
]

By 13 May 2004 when he was back in Red Deer he thinks he received
vegetarian food. He claimed the CRC has been a problem up until his sentencing
hearing started 4 April 2005. Chan said part of the problem is that, whenever
he is transferred back to the CRC, he has to advise them of his vegetarian
diet.

[
62
]

In terms of the effect on him of not receiving a religious diet, Chan
said it made him feel like they were belittling him and he felt he was not
being treated properly as a human being. He said he felt mentally and
physically weak.

[
63
]

In response to the religious diet issue, McNaughton said, once Father
Blanch approved Chan’s request, “we eventually got it right”. A menu was
prepared for Chan with input from a nutritionist. In terms of the CRC’s
response, Canning agreed that it was unreasonable that Chan was not allowed a
religious diet after the Chaplain asked it be given. He said the CRC
misunderstood the policy about religious conversion. The Crown’s submission on
this point is that correctional institutions have a valid concern about
insincere conversions because inmates sometimes use religious conversion as a
way to receive a diet that caters to their food preferences; in a large
institution too many special requests can create administrative difficulties.

[
64
]

Based on the testimony of Li, the note from Father Blanch and Chan’s own
testimony, I believe that Chan’s requests for a vegetarian meal for religious
reasons were sincere. While there is no evidence that the CRC acted with malice
towards Chan, their response fell far short of the mark. Far more effort was
put into resisting his request than would have been necessary for compliance.

[
65
]

Part of the problem was Chan’s response to the question about religion
when he first entered the facility. Correctional authorities do have the right
to question whether dietary requests are really for religious or health
reasons. However, they have no right to tell an inmate that they do not
recognize religious conversion. By March 2004, when Father Blanch said he
believed Chan was being sincere, Chan should have been given a vegetarian diet.
I accept Chan’s testimony that he was not receiving a vegetarian diet until he
was in the RDRC in May 2004. I also accept that, other than administrative
problems, the CRC was at least willing to provide a vegetarian diet to Chan by
May 2004. Part of the problems at the CRC were due to it being a much larger
institution that the RDRC; however, this does not explain their misguided
resistance to his requests. While the deficiency has been cured, it certainly
was treatment that went far beyond the typically harsh conditions in remand.

6.         Religious
Items

[
66
]

Chan testified that he was not allowed prayer beads or incense in his
cell. He also said there were occasions when he was told the only religious
material he could bring into disciplinary segregation or OB’s was a Bible. He
testified that Officer Labello told him that he was not allowed to bring a
prayer card into disciplinary segregation and said that “if it was not a Bible
it was not religious”. Relating to Officer Labello, it is conceded that he
called Chan a “chink”. On a request for interview form dated 2 April 2005, Chan
asked to have his religious material in OB’s. The reply from Deputy Director of
Security Parken was: “The only item approved for OB’s is a Bible, which you
have.”

[
67
]

In terms of the prayer beads, Canning and McNaughton expressed concern
that metal beads could be used as projectiles. Canning said one of the
religious calendars was not allowed because the binding could have been used to
make a key. Canning said that incense is not allowed in inmates’ cells because
the cells are smoke-free and burning incense could set off an alarm. Canning
said in disciplinary segregation inmates are entitled to a Bible or religious
book and that comments otherwise were isolated incidents.

[
68
]

The comments from Officer Labello and Parken were not suitable or proper.
Officer Labello was disciplined by the CRC for making the racial slur. I accept
Canning’s testimony that these were isolated incidents. In terms of Chan’s
testimony concerning prayer beads and incense, I am satisfied with the
responses to these issues and give no credence to the complaints. Security
concerns are an important consideration.

7.         Visits/Phones

[
69
]

Similar to the complaint headed “Denial of Communication with Counsel”,
Chan testified that when the new phone system was in operation it was expensive
for his mother to take these collect calls and he was unable to call her cell
phone number. Chan testified that during the months of the new phone system he
felt completely cut off from family and friends. This system has been changed.
See
Criminal Trial Lawyers’ Assn.

[
70
]

On the issue of visits, Chan testified that visits in the CRC are always
from behind glass. He said during one visit with his mother he was put in belly
chains. His mother Naymee Lum said she was very disturbed to see him like this.

[
71
]

In response Canning agreed that belly chains should have been removed
during Chan’s behind-glass visit with his mother. McNaughton said that visits
are behind glass because of concern about contraband.

[
72
]

I am satisfied there is a good reason for behind-glass visits and I am
not prepared to second guess remand authorities. However, the complaints about
the phone system and belly chains have some merit beyond hard time.

8.         Exercise/Recreation/Media/Fresh
Air

[
73
]

Chan testified that the exercise yard was small and barren, the
television in the common area was black-and-white and there were few books in
the library. He emphasized in his testimony that it was upsetting not to be
allowed access to the gym or weight pit while in administrative segregation.

[
74
]

Victor Barasso, another inmate who was the unit cleaner in the
disciplinary segregation unit, testified that he saw another inmate named Mike
Ferguson receive special treatment while in administrative segregation. Barasso
said he saw Ferguson being given Timbits and McDonald’s food by the guards. He
said he regularly saw Ferguson working out in the weight pit, something he has
not observed being made available to other administrative segregation inmates.

[
75
]

McNaughton agreed that Chan has not been able to use the gymnasium on
more than one or two occasions. Canning said the issue of special treatment for
Ferguson was never investigated. He agreed that giving special treatment to
Ferguson while in administrative segregation in view of other prisoners “as a
peace officer would be reprehensible”.

[
76
]

Given the testimony above and the CRC’s lack of response to the
allegation of special treatment, I conclude that special treatment for Ferguson
did occur, to which I will refer later in my Reasons.

[
77
]

While I acknowledged that administrative segregation inmates do pose
special security concerns, Chan’s lack of access to the weight pit and
gymnasium goes beyond hard time. As to the small and barren exercise yard,
black-and-white television and poor library, these are part of hard time.

9.         Indoor
Air Quality

[
78
]

Chan identified himself as a non-smoker and complained that he was
placed with a smoker for several weeks prior to September 2004, when smoking
was banned. He also expressed concern about the lack of air circulation in the
cells.

[
79
]

In response Canning testified that there is a functioning filtration
system and that maintenance workers change the filters on a regular basis.

[
80
]

I am satisfied with Canning’s response and give no credence to this
complaint.

10.       Temperature

[
81
]

Very little evidence was led on this issue other than Chan saying he has
noticed that cells are usually cold throughout the year. Without more, I can
give no credence to this complaint.

11.       Food

[
82
]

Chan testified that food, particularly at the CRC, was low quality, and
there were long periods of non-eating on the weekend due to only two meals
being served. He also testified that a doctor directed that he receive a
milk-free diet. He said that he has had ongoing problems receiving a milk-free
diet. He admitted that at one time he made a request to the Ombudsman for a
Chinese food diet.

[
83
]

McNaughton testified that since June 2004 prisoners receive a peanut
butter sandwich between their final meal at 4:30 p.m. on Friday and brunch the
next day. Canning agreed that the food at the CRC is something he would not
want to eat every day and that keeping it hot is a challenge.

[
84
]

I have no doubt that even by institutional standards food quality is a
concern: however, it is part of hard time.

12.       Sanitation/Hygiene

[
85
]

Chan said that cleanliness was a concern for him. He made several
complaints about soap not being available such as when he was placed in the
suicide ward.

[
86
]

McNaughton said he was satisfied with the state of cleanliness, and
Canning said there is always soap in the shower.

[
87
]

I am satisfied with the response on this issue and give the complaint no
credence.

13.       Health
Care

[
88
]

Chan testified that he had health problems including colds, flu and
being treated for assault while in remand. He said the conditions in remand
have aggravated his back pain. He said he complained to the College of
Physicians and Surgeons about Dr. Gillespie’s manner. On one occasion Chan
asked for a second medical opinion and was transported the next day from
Calgary to Peace River.

[
89
]

On cross-examination, Chan did not dispute there were 63 entry dates in
the Doctor’s Examination Orders since 2003. He agreed that while in remand he
has received skin cream for a rash, antibiotics, dandruff shampoo, dental care
and an eye exam.

[
90
]

Block testified that rather than saying he was depressed Chan would
translate the symptoms of a mental disorder into tangible physical symptoms.

[
91
]

Canning agreed that it was not Chan’s choice to go from Calgary to Peace
River for a second medical opinion.

[
92
]

In terms of medical care, Chan was never denied medical treatment, even
for minor concerns, whether for tangible physical symptoms of a mental disorder
or otherwise. Chan’s access to medical services was as good as or better than
most individuals receive outside of remand. Thus, I give no credence to this
complaint. I will deal with the Peace River transfer issue under the heading
“Transport/A & D Holding Cells”.

14.       Clothing

[
93
]

The primary complaint concerns Calgary male remand inmates being
required to wear blue overalls and prison-issued runners while female inmate
prisoners wear sweat pants and t‑shirts. Chan testified that before he
was in remand he was prescribed orthotic shoes because of chronic back pain but
he was not allowed to wear them in remand.

[
94
]

Canning confirmed that Chan was correct that women are allowed to wear
track suits. In terms of shoes, Canning said that runners are prison-issued
because there was at least one occasion where an inmate carried cannabis and a
needle in a non-prison issued running shoe. He agreed there were complaints
about the quality of the runners.

[
95
]

I accept that prison-issued runners address legitimate security
concerns. While blue overalls and prison-issued runners are not the most
comfortable clothing choice, this is part of hard time.

15.       Bedding/Bed

[
96
]

Chan said the mattresses in remand were thin and that he was sometimes
cold because he did not receive enough blankets. McNaughton agreed that the
mattresses are thin but said prisoners can get more than one blanket as a
matter of routine. In the result, I give no credence to this complaint.

16.       Work
for Pay

[
97
]

Chan testified that female inmates were paid to put condiments in trays.
This employment was not available to male inmates. Canning agreed that a few
female inmates are paid a nominal fee for bagging condiments. He explained this
is a small program. I accept Canning’s explanation and give no credence to this
complaint.

17.       Education/Programs

[
98
]

Testimony by Chan on this issue was that, while he was able to buy
educational material at the RDRC, when he asked for books or tried to seek
education in Calgary he was told nothing was offered. Canning agreed that he
has never seen an expenditure out of the CRC’s budget for educational
materials. Chan said he has seen sentenced inmates in Peace River who were able
to go to school while in remand.

[
99
]

While it would be beneficial to offer more programs to unsentenced
inmates who are in remand for long periods of time, I acknowledge that it is
difficult for remand authorities to predict how long an inmate will be in custody.

aspects of hard time.

18.       Cultural/Media

[
100
]

Chan
testified that in Calgary, other than in disciplinary segregation where there
was no radio, inmates could listen to one of five or six pre-programmed
channels. When he asked about listening to a Chinese radio station he was told
that there are 400 people in the CRC and the majority decide the radio
stations. He also said that he had difficulty at both the CRC and the RDRC getting
clearance on Chinese books that had been dropped off. On 1 March 2005, when he
requested that Chinese books be brought into the CRC, the reply he received to
the request for interview form was: “English and French are the languages of
the land.”

[
101
]

Remand
authorities did not respond specifically to the radio and book complaints other
than Canning saying that books can be a security concern because they can be
used for smuggling contraband. While I am not entirely satisfied with this response,
these restrictions are part of hard time.

19.       Removing
Compatibles

[
102
]

Chan’s
only evidence was that once in the RDRC he was bunked with a roommate with whom
he was very compatible. This roommate was later transferred to another cell. I
give no credence to this complaint because it is not up to Chan to pick his
roommates.

20.       Privacy

[
103
]

This
complaint centred on the lack of privacy Chan says he experienced when using
the toilet in his cell. At one point he said the RDRC gave him a bed sheet to
allow him some privacy. I am giving no credence to this complaint because the
lack of privacy is legitimately tied to security concerns.

21.       Transport/A
& D Holding Cells

[
104
]

Exhibit
46 details approximately 50 one-way trips involving Chan that occurred between
remand centres. During these trips he was transported in a variety of prison
vehicles where he said he was hunched over with his ankles shackled and
handcuffs on. He was also required at times to wear belly chains so that he
could not lift his hands to his face. He expressed concern about his safety in

other inmates. He said that by the time the trips in the van were completed he
experienced a lot of neck and back pain. An engineer’s report by Brian Thicke
reviewed the safety of the prison vans and was submitted as part of the
evidence in this case.

[
105
]

In
terms of comparing provincial correctional transportation to the federal
system, Bentenuto testified that federal inmates wore seatbelts but that a
majority of the seats were not cushioned and are not made for luxurious trips.

[
106
]

I
accept that the prison vans have to be designed to ensure inmates are kept
secure and they are not necessarily designed for comfort. Inmate safety is a
very important issue; however, it is not up to this Court to determine what an
appropriate correctional transport van design should be. Thus, I give no
credence to this complaint.

[
107
]

In
terms of the evidence about Chan being transferred from Calgary to Peace River
when he asked for a second medical opinion, Canning does not deny that this
occurred and agrees there was no reason to refer him to a doctor in Peace
River. The Crown’s submission is that the reason Chan was transferred could
have been to give the CRC a break and to allow a cooling off period for both
sides.

[
108
]

I
can accept that a cooling off period is within the discretion of remand
authorities, but, even if this was the correct explanation, it does not justify
sending Chan on an uncomfortable trip to Peace River. This goes beyond hard
time.

22.       Excessive
Force/Lockup

[
109
]

On
the excessive force issue Chan testified that he was assaulted on several
occasions. He said in October 2004 Officer Bush assaulted him while he was
being admitted to the CRC. Chan said that when he would not spread his buttock
cheeks during a strip search, Officer Bush threatened him with pepper spray and
forced him to the ground. Eventually a senior officer intervened.

[
110
]

Canning
conceded this incident did occur and agreed that Officer Bush was not following
correct procedure when he intervened physically. While conceding that
unauthorized application of force occurred, the Crown points out that a senior
officer intervened quickly and if Chan had any injuries they were relatively
minor in nature. I accept the validity of this point; nevertheless, this is an
incident that goes beyond hard time.

[
111
]

Chan
alleged that he was assaulted on 21 March 2005 by CAPS Officer Posch at the
Edmonton Remand Centre before a Court appearance. At the time Chan said he was
using a towel for underwear because the underwear he was provided was not
clean. He said Officer Posch felt the towel during a pat down search and then
ordered Chan to strip. Chan said he cooperated with the strip search but
refused Officer Posch’s request to bend over and spread his buttock cheeks.
Chan said the request was repeated and he again refused. Chan said Officer
Posch then grabbed his right wrist and in response Chan struggled and pushed
away. Chan said next a bunch of guards came in and he was punched on the back
of the head and thrown to the ground. He said he was put in a heavy canvas
garment and dragged through the corridors and later treated at an Edmonton
hospital.

[
112
]

Concerning
the 21 March 2005 incident, Officer Posch testified that he felt a bulge when
he was patting down Chan’s torso and became suspicious. Once he decided to do
the strip search he proceeded to do a full strip search. Chan would not comply

[

]

Second,
although Block spent a good deal of time with Chan, and administered many tests

[

At approximately 1721 hours I
opened [inmate] Chan’s cell to have him return the supper tray. At this time

until code team arrived and broke up fight.

[
145
]

I
have not been given any explanation as to this remarkable coincidence, that is,
that the man who shot Chan’s friend in December 2002 would assault Chan

[
146
]

I am not prepared to find that Chan’s psychological problems are

[
147
]

A
further issue arose from Block’s report. At pp. 12-13 of his report, Block
stated:

Of particular concern at this
point is how others are apt to perceive him in his current state. That is, his
symptoms arising from the negative experiences in Remand will invariably alter

demeanor and body language. Thus, he may well be at a disadvantage because

reflective of negativity, lying, or implied guilt. First impressions will be
particularly indelible with negative associations likely derived in those
encountering him for the first time. This may explain the punitive actions
taken by the Remand staff.

Chan already provided testimony
in his defense and was disbelieved. If he provides further testimony, he is apt
to be scrutinized on the manner in which he replies to questions, facial
expressions, tone of voice, physical movements, general integrity,
intelligence, and powers of recollection. Assessments of credibility are
influenced by a person’s demeanor. These are partly subjective in nature, but
if the person appears to lack spontaneity, frankness, or is prone to
hesitation, this is apt to leave a misleading impression.

Personality traits, cultural
background, and his psychological condition arising out of the traumatic prison
experience seem to best explain his style of presentation. For example, lack of
eye contact, hesitation and inconsistency, unusual reasoning, and under-or-over
elaboration may contribute to “proof” that he is lying when, in actuality, this
is more reflective of mental illness. Many people unwittingly subscribe to
stereotypical views on credibility leading to unfounded inferences, which lack
objective bases.

[
148
]

The
Crown objects to these portions of his report as being oath-helping. The rule
against oath-helping is described at 11:20:50 of
McWilliam’s Canadian
Criminal Evidence
, 4th ed. looseleaf (Aurora, Ont.: Canada Law Book, 2005):

The rule against oath-helping
precludes a party from leading evidence whose
sole
purpose is to bolster
the general credibility of a witness. [Emphasis in original. Footnote omitted.]

[
149
]

This
proffered testimony usurps my role to assess and determine credibility, and I
reject it.

]

III.       Charter
Arguments

[
153
]

Chan
alleges that rights guaranteed to him by the
Charter
have been
infringed or denied. The rights alleged to have been infringed or denied are
ss. 2(a), 7, 8, 9, 10(b), 11(d), 12 and 15. If I find one or more
Charter

breaches, Chan is requesting a stay of proceedings or a drastic reduction in
sentence for his heroin trafficking and possession of the proceeds of crime
convictions.

A.        Section
2(a)

[
154
]

Section
2(a) of the
Charter
reads:

2. Everyone has the following
fundamental freedoms:

(a)        freedom
of conscience and religion; ...

[
155
]

Chan
claims he was denied the right to worship and practise Buddhism and Taoism
because he was denied a vegetarian diet and was not allowed access to his
prayer beads or incense while in remand. He also claims that he was not allowed
his religious materials in disciplinary segregation. Chan cites
R. v. Big
M Drug Mart Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, where Dickson J. defined
freedom of religion at 336 as follows:

The essence of the concept of
freedom of religion is the right to entertain such religious beliefs as a
person chooses, the right to declare religious beliefs openly and without fear
of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to manifest religious belief by worship
and practice or by teaching and dissemination.

[
156
]

Chan
also cites
Maurice v. Canada (Attorney General)
(2002),
2002 FCT 69 (CanLII)
, 210
D.L.R. (4th) 186 (F.C.T.D.),

in support of an inmate’s entitlement to a
religious diet. In
Maurice
, the inmate had renounced the Hare
Krishna faith but still claimed an entitlement to a vegetarian diet based on
freedom of conscience. The Court agreed, noting that this was no real burden on
the institution because it already provided vegetarian meals to inmates based
on religious beliefs.

[
157
]

The
Crown responds to the s. 2(a) argument using the framework from
Syndicat
Northcrest v. Amselem
, [2004] 2 S.C.R. 551,
2004 SCC 47
. In that case,
the appellants set up succahs on their condominium balconies for the purpose of
fulfilling the biblically mandated obligation of dwelling during the annual
nine-day Jewish religious festival of Succot. The majority of the Court, per
Iacobucci J., found that stipulations in the declaration of co-ownership
infringed the appellants’ freedom of religion under s. 3 of the Quebec
Charter
.
In so finding, Iacobucci J. set out the principles that are applicable when an
individual alleges an infringement of his or her freedom of religion under the
Quebec
Charter
or the
Charter
.

[
158
]

Iacobucci
J. summarized the analysis applicable to an allegation of an infringement of
freedom of religion at para. 65:

[T]he first step in successfully
advancing a claim that an individual’s freedom of religion has been infringed
is for a claimant to demonstrate that he or she sincerely believes in a practice
or belief that has a nexus with religion. The second step is to then
demonstrate that the impugned conduct of a third party interferes with the
individual’s ability to act in accordance with that practice or belief in a
manner that is non‑trivial.

[
159
]

Concerning
the first step, Iacobucci J. stated at para. 43 that “[t]he emphasis ... is on
personal choice of religious beliefs”. At para. 46, he summarized:

[O]ur Court’s past decisions and
the basic principles underlying freedom of religion support the view that
freedom of religion consists of the freedom to undertake practices and harbour
beliefs, having a nexus with religion, in which an individual demonstrates he
or she sincerely believes or is sincerely undertaking in order to connect with
the divine or as a function of his or her spiritual faith, irrespective of
whether a particular practice or belief is required by official religious dogma
or is in conformity with the position of religious officials.

[
160
]

At
para. 54, Iacobucci J. said that it is unnecessary to adduce expert evidence to
demonstrate that an individual’s belief or practice conforms with the belief or
practice of other adherents of a particular religion, although an individual
may choose to adduce such evidence for the purpose of demonstrating sincerity.
He noted, at para. 53, that a court’s inquiry into sincerity should not focus
on past practice or past belief and further, at para. 17, that it could not be
concluded that an individual’s beliefs were not sincere just because he or she
previously celebrated his or her religion differently. “Sincerity of belief at
the relevant time is the governing standard”:
Syndicat Northcrest

at para.
71
.

[
161
]

Concerning
the second step, Iacobucci J. stated at para. 58 that
s. 2
(a) of the
Charter

“prohibits only burdens or impositions on religious practice that are
non-trivial”. To determine whether interference is more than trivial or
insubstantial, the context of each case must be examined. In relation to
examining the context, Iacobucci J. emphasized that the rights of others must
always be taken into account, saying at para. 61:

In this respect, it should be
emphasized that not every action will become summarily unassailable and receive
automatic protection under the banner of freedom of religion. No right,
including freedom of religion, is absolute.... This is so because we live in a
society of individuals in which we must always take the rights of others into
account.... In the real world, oftentimes the fundamental rights of individuals
will conflict or compete with one another.

[
162
]

Turning
to Chan’s allegation of infringement of his freedom of religion, the relevant
facts are detailed under the headings “Religious Diet” and “Religious Items”.

[
163
]

Applying
the two-part test set out in
Syndicat Northcrest

to those
facts, I first consider whether Chan has demonstrated that he sincerely
believes in a practice or belief that has a nexus with religion. I find that
Chan’s religious beliefs are sincere and that he sincerely believes that certain
practices centring on a vegetarian diet, prayer beads, religious books and
incense are experientially religious in nature. Li’s testimony and the note
from Father Blanch provide support for that finding. It was unnecessary
for Li to have testified that she does not believe there is any harm in
believing in Buddhism, Chinese Taoism and Confucianism. It was made clear by
Iacobucci J. in
Syndicat Northcrest
that religious beliefs are a
matter of personal choice. Moreover, just because Chan ate meat during his
first stay in remand does not mean he was insincere about following a Buddhist
diet in 2004. Again, it was made clear by Iacobucci J. in
Syndicat
Northcrest
that my inquiry as to sincerity should not be past-focused.
In the result, I find that the first part of the test has been met.

[
164
]

Applying
the second part of the test, I consider whether Chan has demonstrated that the
impugned government conduct interfered with his ability to act in accordance
with his religious practices or beliefs in a manner that was non-trivial. I
consider first that Chan was not allowed prayer beads and incense in his cell.
There was testimony that the beads could be used as projectiles, which I
acknowledge is a legitimate security concern in a remand setting. Using incense
inside a cell is clearly a fire hazard. Moreover, it could impact on the air
quality in the close quarters in remand. In
Syndicat Northcrest
,
Iacobucci J. emphasized that the context, including the rights of others, must
be examined in determining whether interference is more than trivial.
Considering the context, including the potential harm to others, I conclude
that the interference in relation to the prayer beads and incense was
insubstantial. Thus, I find no infringement in relation to the prayer beads and
incense.

[
165
]

I
next consider Chan’s complaint that he was denied access to his religious
material when he was placed in disciplinary segregation and OB’s. I accepted
Canning’s testimony that these were isolated incidents and that a religious
calendar’s binding raised security concerns. Considering the context, including
the potential harm to others, I conclude that the interference in relation to
the religious material was also insubstantial. Therefore, I find no
infringement in relation to the religious material.

[
166
]

Finally,
I consider Chan’s complaint that, while in remand, he was denied a religion‑based
vegetarian diet for a considerable period of time. I concede that the CRC is
significantly larger than the RDRC and that it could take some time to get a
special food order right. However, the CRC’s refusal to provide a vegetarian
diet to Chan amounted to more than administrative difficulty or oversight. In
fact, a senior remand official at the CRC explained this refusal by telling
Chan they do not recognize religious conversions. The CRC subsequently directed
that the RDRC stop providing a vegetarian diet to Chan. I am particularly
troubled by the CRC’s refusal to accept a request from Father Blanch that
Chan’s request for a meat-free diet be accepted. In fact, Canning agreed it was
unreasonable that Chan was not allowed a religious diet after the Chaplain
requested this for him. The nurse’s chart entry that Chan be placed in a
baby-doll because he was on a hunger strike is equally troubling. I accept that
by May 2004 Chan was generally receiving vegetarian meals. Regardless, this
adds up to more than four months where his repeated requests were either denied
or proactively thwarted. I accept Chan’s testimony that he felt belittled and
improperly treated as a human being. I also accept that being denied a
religious diet made him feel mentally and physically weak. Considering the
context, I have no hesitation in finding that the denial of a religion-based
vegetarian diet interfered with Chan’s freedom of religion in a substantial
way. In consequence, I find that Chan has made out an infringement of his
freedom of religion as guaranteed by
s. 2
(a) of the
Charter
.

[
167
]

Having
found an infringement, and assuming that the impugned government conduct is a
limit “prescribed by law”, I must consider whether the infringement can be
saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
. While the Crown has the burden of
proving justification under s. 1, the Crown did no more than make passing
reference to the applicable four-part test in
R. v. Oakes
,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986]
1 S.C.R. 103.

[
168
]

At
the first step of the
Oakes
test, it must be determined if the
government conduct is pursuing a sufficiently important objective to justify
limiting a
Charter
right. The CRC’s objective is to avoid being
forced to provide special meals that do not have a true religious basis. This
is a sufficiently important objective.

[
169
]

The
second step is to determine if there is a rational connection between the
government conduct and the objective. I do not take issue with the CRC requiring
some evidence of the sincerity of an inmate’s religious beliefs when there has
been a dietary request for religious reasons. However, the actions taken by the
CRC in the first four months of 2004 were directed at resisting Chan’s request
for a vegetarian diet, not at making a reasonable attempt to ensure his request
had a sincere religious basis. Indeed, Canning admitted that it was
unreasonable that Chan was not allowed a religious diet after the Chaplain
requested this for him. Having found that the second step is not satisfied,
there is no need to continue the
Oakes

analysis. The s.
2(a) violation is not saved by s. 1.

B.

Section
7

[
170
]

Section
7
of the
Charter
reads:

7. Everyone has the right to
life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived
thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

[
171
]

Chan
alleges that several of the 28 categorized complaints are violations of s. 7.
I will focus on those complaints to which Counsel for Chan has made more than
passing reference. This same approach will be used in relation to alleged
violations of ss. 8, 9, 10(b), 11(d), 12 and 15.

[
172
]

Chan
alleges his security of the person has been violated. A two-step analysis must
be undertaken in response to an allegation of an infringement of s. 7. First,
it must be determined whether the government conduct at issue constituted a
deprivation of security of the person. Second, if there has been a deprivation,
it must be ascertained whether the deprivation was effected in accordance with
the principles of fundamental justice.

[
173
]

Chan’s
first s. 7 complaint is that he was denied proper medical treatment in remand.
The leading case on the
Charter
implications of denying medical
treatment is
R. v. Morgentaler
,
1988 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 30,

where
a majority of the Court held that the restrictions in the
Criminal Code

on abortion were a risk to health and therefore a deprivation of security of
the person. However, as previously noted, there is no evidentiary basis for
this complaint. While in remand, Chan was never denied medical treatment, even
for minor concerns. There are 63 entry dates in relation to Chan in the
Doctor’s Examination Orders since 2003.

[
174
]

Other
complaints that are said to involve a breach of Chan’s security of the person
are the trip from the CRC to the Peace River Remand Centre for a second medical
opinion and his denial of or limited contact with family and friends during the
period of the new collect call phone system in remand. While the former was an
uncomfortable trip, I cannot characterize it as a risk to his health so as to
engage s. 7. See
Morgentaler
. Further, I cannot characterize the
latter as having a serious and profound effect on Chan’s psychological
integrity so as to engage s. 7. See
New Brunswick (Minister of Health and
Community Services) v. G.(J.)
,
1999 CanLII 653 (SCC)
, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 46 at para.
60
.

[
175
]

Chan’s
final claim concerning s. 7 is that the assaults he endured had a severe impact
on his physical and psychological well-being and therefore violated his
security of the person. As to the impact on Chan’s physical well-being, Counsel
for Chan provided no authority to support this proposition, nor did he develop
it. In the circumstances, I decline to address this issue.

[
176
]

As
to the impact on Chan’s psychological well-being, the Crown agrees that
security of the person includes psychological integrity. While it is true that
the meaning of security of the person has been expanded to include psychological
integrity, the majority of the Court in
G.(J.)
stated at para.

60
:

For a restriction of security of
the person to be made out, then, the impugned state action must have a serious
and profound effect on a person’s psychological integrity. The effects of the
state interference must be assessed objectively, with a view to their impact on
the psychological integrity of a person of reasonable sensibility. This need
not rise to the level of nervous shock or psychiatric illness, but must be
greater than ordinary stress or anxiety.

[
177
]

The
issue here is whether two applications of force in the context of strip
searches had a serious and profound effect on Chan’s psychological integrity.
Chan’s primary contention in this regard is that he suffered post‑traumatic
stress disorder as a result of being in remand, with particular reference to
the applications of force. However, there is no or insufficient cogent evidence
to support this theory. The psychological harm must result from the impugned government
conduct. However, as I have indicated, I am not prepared to find that Chan’s
psychological problems are because of ill-treatment while in remand. Chan’s
causation problems are similar to those detailed in
Blencoe v. British
Columbia (Human Rights Commission)
, [2000] 2 S.C.R. 307,
2000 SCC 44
.
Given Chan’s inability to establish a deprivation of security of the person, as
required at the first step of the s. 7 analysis, I need not address the second
step of the analysis.

C.        Section
8

[
178
]

Section
8
of the
Charter
reads:

8. Everyone has the right to be
secure against unreasonable search or seizure.

[
179
]

Chan
contends that he found strip searches to be degrading and dehumanizing and that
he felt violated by them. He further contends that the two applications of
force he experienced while being strip searched amounted to s. 8 violations.

[
180
]

As
stated at para. 44, in
R. v. Golden
, [2001] 3 S.C.R. 679,
2001
SCC 83
, to determine whether there is a violation of s. 8, a court must answer
the following three questions:

(1) Was the search authorized by
law?

(2) Is the law itself reasonable?

(3) Was the search conducted in a
reasonable manner?

If the answer to each of these questions is yes, then there
is no s. 8 violation.

[
181
]

On
the issue of whether searches in the context of a remand centre are authorized
by law, the answer is yes. As previously discussed,
s.10
of the
Correctional
Institution Regulation
provides authority for any manner of searches.
There is also common law authority for strip searches of inmates entering a
prison population. See
Golden
at para.
96
.

[
182
]

Is
the law which authorizes strip searches in a remand centre reasonable? The
Supreme Court in
Weatherall v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
1993 CanLII 112 (SCC)
, [1993]
2 S.C.R. 872, stated at 877: “Imprisonment necessarily entails surveillance,
searching and scrutiny.” I heard evidence, which I accept, that remand inmates
conceal weapons and drugs on their persons. I am satisfied that full strip
searches are necessary for the protection of both correctional staff and remand
inmates. In the result, the law is reasonable.

[
183
]

Finally,
I must decide if the strip searches, apart from the two strip searches
involving application of force, were conducted in a reasonable manner. The
reasoning expressed in
Weatherall
which dealt with inmate privacy
concerns about cell inspections and frisk searches has application here. The
Court, per La Forest J., stated at 877: “A substantially reduced level of
privacy is present in this setting and a prisoner thus cannot hold a reasonable
expectation of privacy with respect to these practices.” Chan’s primary
complaint during strip searches was that the CRC guards requested he spread his
buttock cheeks and lift his scrotum. Given the necessity of thorough searches,
strip searches conducted in accordance with such requests were conducted in a
reasonable manner. As was pointed out during the evidence of correction
officials, conducting strip searches is an unpleasant but necessary aspect of a
guard’s job.

[
184
]

In
terms of the clothing exchange I do not find this practice to constitute an
unreasonable search. I am satisfied that this practice is utilized with due
regard for the inmates’ dignity.

[
185
]

The
final issue to address are the two applications of force Chan experienced in
the context of strip searches. In light of the application of physical force,
were these two strip searches of Chan conducted in a reasonable manner? On this
point, these applications of physical force were clearly not reasonable. The
correction officers did not follow procedure which called for isolating Chan in
a cell and did not authorize force. While force was not authorized, there is a
distinction between unauthorized applications of force which occurred when Chan
did not comply with strip search requests and the strip searches themselves
which, I find, were conducted in a reasonable manner.

[
186
]

As
I have answered all three questions affirmatively in respect of all strip
searches, it follows that I find no violation of s. 8.

D.        Section
9

[
187
]

Section
9
of the
Charter
reads:

9. Everyone has the right not to
be arbitrarily detained or imprisoned.

[
188
]

While
Counsel for Chan is not questioning Chan’s detention, he takes issue with
disciplinary hearings while in remand. He submits that the hearings were
grossly unfair and in some instances resulted in punishments of time in
disciplinary segregation.

[
189
]

Commenting
on the scope of s. 9 in
Constitutional Law of Canada
, 4th ed. looseleaf
(Toronto: Carswell, 1997) at 46-2, Peter W. Hogg states that there must be a
detention or imprisonment and it must be arbitrary.

[
190
]

The
Crown agrees that a remand disciplinary regime could properly fall under s. 9.
However, the Crown argues that, even with the relaxed standard established in
Weaver
,
it is questionable whether there is any connection between this alleged
Charter

violation and the charges before the Court. The disciplinary hearings were said
to be in response to intervening incidents that arose during Chan’s
imprisonment and not his imprisonment itself. I agree with the Crown’s
submission.

[
191
]

In
the event that I am wrong in so agreeing, I will go on to consider whether the
disciplinary proceedings were arbitrary. On this issue I refer to my comments
under the heading “Disciplinary Hearings”. I am comfortable that rules of
procedural fairness are normally being followed in these hearings. Thus, while
there may be flaws in the process, these hearings are not arbitrary. I find no
