E.         Section
10(b)

[
192
]

Section
10
(b) of the
Charter
reads:

10. Everyone has the right on
arrest or detention ...

(b)        to
retain and instruct counsel without delay and to be informed of that right; ...

[
193
]

Chan
claims his ability to contact counsel was denied or made difficult during the
period when the new phone system was implemented in remand. He argues that this
falls under
s.10
(b) because he was detained.

[
194
]

While
I agree there were phone problems, as discussed under the heading “Denial of
Communication with Counsel”, there is a difference between a person not being
given a reasonable opportunity to retain and instruct counsel without delay and
a person being unable to have almost daily conversations with retained counsel
about the progress of his or her case. The latter appeared to be the issue
here. Thus, I find no violation of
s. 10
(b).

F.         Section
11(d)

[
195
]

Section
11
(d) of the
Charter
reads:

11. Any person charged with an
offence has the right ...

(d)        to
be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law in a fair and public
hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal; ...

[
196
]

I
am unable to locate any reference to s. 11(d) in the written brief of Counsel
for Chan, and I heard only passing reference to it in oral argument.
Nevertheless, the first argument under s. 11(d) appears to be that Chan was
denied a fair trial because his demeanour was impacted by his treatment in
remand. I have already dealt with this issue, and in my opinion this argument
has no merit and is not a violation of s. 11(d).

[
197
]

Chan’s
next argument is that the disciplinary hearing process which he was party to
while in remand violated s. 11(d). In
R. v. Wigglesworth
,
1987 CanLII 41 (SCC)
, [1987]
2 S.C.R. 541 at 561, Wilson J., for the majority, outlined the scope of s.
11(d):

In my opinion, a true penal
consequence which would attract the application of s. 11 is imprisonment
or a fine which by its magnitude would appear to be imposed for the purpose of
redressing the wrong done to society at large rather than the maintenance of
internal discipline within the limited sphere of activity.

Relating this to a remand centre, Chan is already being held
in custody. Canning testified that the purpose of disciplinary hearings was to
maintain order in the CRC and if rules were broken to impose consequences on
offenders. In my view the disciplinary hearings in remand are designed to
maintain internal discipline and fall outside the scope of s. 11(d).

[
198
]

It
should also be noted that s. 11(d) refers to a “public hearing”, which is not
necessarily appropriate in a remand setting.

[
199
]

Finally,
under s. 11(d), Counsel for Chan submits that Chan’s ability to contact counsel
was made difficult during the period of the new phone system. This is said to
have breached his right to a fair trial before Moore J. This argument was
rejected earlier, and I reject it for the same reason in the context of s.
11(d). Thus, I find no violation of s. 11(d).

G.        Section
12

[
200
]

Section
12
of the
Charter
reads:

12. Everyone has the right not to
be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[
201
]

Chan’s
submissions on this point are that either individually or cumulatively his
treatment while in remand, including frequent transport while restrained,
wearing a baby-doll, disciplinary segregation, strip searches and unauthorized
applications of physical force, amounted to cruel and unusual treatment or
punishment.

[
202
]

R.
v. Smith
,
1987 CanLII 64 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 1045 at 1072, referring to a decision of
Laskin C.J. in
R. v. Miller
,
1976 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 680, sets out the
test for determining if punishment is cruel and unusual, namely, “whether the
punishment prescribed is so excessive as to outrage standards of decency”.
While the state may impose punishment, “the effect of that punishment must not
be grossly disproportionate to what would have been appropriate”:
Smith

at 1072.

[
203
]

Hogg
states at 50-11 that s. 12 can apply not only to penalties prescribed by the
Criminal
Code
or other statutes creating offences but also to oppressive
conditions in prisons such as overcrowding.

[
204
]

Chan
cites
Trang v. Alberta (Director of the Edmonton Remand Centre)

(2001), 298 A.R. 149 at para.
20
,
2001 ABQB 659
, where Marceau J., in
determining that there were serious issues to be tried, endorsed the argument
that cumulative conditions could lead to a s. 12 violation. In
Munoz v.
Alberta (Edmonton Remand Centre)
,
2004 ABQB 769
at para.
78
, Nation J.
concluded that the treatment at Edmonton Remand Centre of the five applicants
did not amount to a s. 12 violation. In
Munoz
, complaints
included being shackled in the exercise yard, being double-bunked in
administrative segregation and the loss of gymnasium privileges.

[
205
]

There
is no question that time in remand is hard, particularly when most inmates are
struggling to cope with harsh conditions while dealing with the stress of their
legal defence. However, it must be recognized that drugs and weapons are a
serious problem in remand and these problems impact conditions. A number of
Chan’s complaints do have merit, particularly the refusal of the CRC to provide
a religious diet. This was addressed under s. 2(a). In aggregate, the
complaints that had merit went beyond hard time and are a reason for enhanced
credit. In my view, while his time has been beyond typical hard time in some
respects, his treatment in remand, viewed globally, does not amount to treatment
that would “outrage standards of decency”.

H.        Section
15

[
206
]

Section
15
of the
Charter
reads:

15.(1) Every individual is equal
before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal
benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without
discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex,
age or mental or physical disability.

(2) Subsection (1) does not
preclude any law, program or activity that has as its object the amelioration
of conditions of disadvantaged individuals or groups including those that are
disadvantaged because of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion,
sex, age or mental or physical disability.

[
207
]

Chan
claims he was not given access to medical care of the same quality or frequency
as others in society not detained in remand. He also complains that some female
inmates at the CRC were allowed to work packing condiments while male inmates
were not. Since there is no evidence he was denied necessary medical treatment
and because I view the condiment complaint as trivial, it is not necessary for
me to engage in a s. 15 analysis. I find no violation of s. 15.

I.          Remedy

[
208
]

If
a
Charter
breach is found, counsel for Chan requests a remedy
under s. 24(1). The remedy requested is a stay, a drastic reduction in sentence
or a remedy otherwise deemed appropriate by this Court. Given that I have found
a breach of s. 2(a), it is necessary that I consider an appropriate remedy
under s. 24(1). It is well-accepted that this section confers a broad
discretion on the Court. See Hogg at 37-29. In

Doe v. Metropolitan
Toronto (Municipality) Commissioners of Police
(1998),
1998 CanLII 14826 (ON CTGD)
, 39 O.R. (3d) 487
(Gen. Div.), McFarland J. made a declaration that the complainant’s
Charter

rights were violated and awarded her damages based on a negligence damage
assessment. MacFarland J. concluded at 527:

In such circumstances the
plaintiff is entitled to one award of damages to compensate her for the damage
she has suffered. She is not, in my view, in these circumstances, entitled to
any additional or “extra” damages because the police conduct has breached her
Charter

rights. In this respect, assuming she is otherwise fully compensated, a
declaration will suffice.

[
209
]

With respect to the violation of
s. 2
(a) of the
Charter

in this case, a just remedy is a declaration that Chan’s freedom of religion
was violated. While the ongoing refusal of the CRC to provide a vegetarian diet
to Chan was a serious breach of his freedom of religion, the issue was finally
resolved and in my opinion the refusal did not arise from any malice
specifically directed at Chan. In these circumstances, I do not consider it
appropriate to stay the proceedings, nor do I believe that a stay of these
proceedings is what the Court in
O’Connor
had in mind when it
referred to the remedy of a stay as “a last resort”. Furthermore, I cannot say
that “irreparable prejudice would be caused to the integrity of the judicial system
if the prosecution were continued”. There is another way of protecting Chan’s
rights, such as by giving him extra credit for pre-sentence custody.

IV.       Credit

for Pre-sentence Custody

A.        Case Law

[
210
]

The
next issue to be considered is the amount of credit to be given to Chan for the
time he has already spent in pre-sentence custody. He has been in pre-sentence
custody since 12 June 2003 until today. This is a total of 26 months
and one day.

[
211
]

Before
addressing credit for pre-sentence custody, it is useful to comment briefly on
the
Bail Reform Act
, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 37. Prior to the
Bail
Reform Act
, bail was left to the discretion of the judge. See
R.
v. Hall
, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 309,
2002 SCC 64
. The
Bail Reform Act

set out specific criteria for denying bail to an accused and replaced the
presumption of pre-trial detention with a presumption of release. Counsel for
Chan has not taken issue with the order of Sullivan J. that he be detained in
custody. In fact, Chan did not make application for bail once he was ordered
detained on the second charges. His counsel submits that it was a foregone
conclusion that he would not be released.

[
212
]

It
is uncontested in view of the discretionary nature of
s. 719(3)
of the
Criminal
Code
that I may give Chan some extra credit for pre-sentence custody.
See
R. v. Wust
, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 455 at para.
41
,
2000 SCC 18
, per
Arbour J:

To maintain that pre-sentencing
custody can never be
deemed
punishment following conviction because the
legal system does not punish innocent people is an exercise in semantics that
does not acknowledge the reality of pre-sentencing custody so carefully
delineated by Laskin J.A., in
Rezaie
,
supra
, and by Gary Trotter
in his text,
The Law of Bail in Canada
(2nd ed. 1999), at p. 37:

Remand prisoners, as they are
sometimes called, often spend their time awaiting trial in detention centres or
local jails that are ill‑suited to lengthy stays. As the Ouimet Report
stressed, such institutions may restrict liberty more than many institutions
which house the convicted. Due to overcrowding, inmate turnover and the
problems of effectively implementing programs and recreation activities,
serving time in such institutions can be quite onerous.

Therefore, while pre-trial
detention is not intended as punishment when it is imposed, it is, in effect,
deemed part of the punishment following the offender’s conviction, by the
operation of s. 719(3). The effect of deeming such detention punishment is not
unlike the determination, discussed earlier in these reasons, that time spent
lawfully at large while on parole is considered nonetheless a continuation of
the offender’s sentence of incarceration. [Emphasis in original.]

[
213
]

The
normal practice of many judges is to give a 2:1 credit. On the specific issue
of a ratio of 2:1, Arbour J. in
Wust
stated at para.
45
:

[M]any judges have given more or
less two months credit for each month spent in pre-sentencing detention. This
is entirely appropriate even though a different ratio could also be applied....

[
214
]

In
terms of the reason for 2:1 credit to be the norm, Côté J.A. in
R. v.
Roberts
, supra,
(2005), 192 C.C.C. (3d) 462 at para.
74
,
2005 ABCA 11
,
stated that the main reason that double credit is the usual practice in Alberta
and not treble is because of statutory remission:

Few prisoners serve their whole
sentence. It is common that they be released between 1/3 and 2/3 of the way
through it. A median between the two points is one-half. Dividing by one-half
yields the common double credit for pre-trial custody....

[
215
]

In
addition to statutory remission, another reason for credit is harsh conditions
and a lack of programs in remand centres. While harsh conditions in remand can
be one of the reasons for enhanced credit, this does not mean the rate of
credit should necessarily increase beyond 2:1. In
Roberts
, the
Court of Appeal reduced the credit for pre-trial custody to double credit from
triple credit. One reason was a lack of evidence tendered about conditions in
the Edmonton Remand Centre.

[
216
]

Counsel
for Chan argues that Chan should receive more than the 2:1 credit commonly
given primarily because of the exceptionally harsh conditions and treatment
that he experienced. He cites
R. v. Taylor
,
2002 ABQB 266
, where
3:1 credit was awarded. In
Taylor
, Veit J. concluded that
conditions in the Peace River and Edmonton Remand Centres were onerous,
specifically focusing on the inability of the defendant to participate in
programs. He had been serving a sentence at the Peace River Correctional
Institution but was transferred to the Peace River Remand Centre after a
robbery charge was later laid against him. Counsel for Chan submits that the
conditions he experienced in his pre-sentence custody went far beyond the
conditions described in
Taylor
.

[
217
]

Another
decision Counsel for Chan cites is
R. v. Ferguson
, [2005] 4
W.W.R. 737,
2004 ABQB 928
. This is the inmate referred to above who, I found to
have received special treatment. The defendant RCMP officer was awarded a
credit of 3:1 for the 70 days he spent in jail awaiting sentencing. Hawco J.
stated at para. 52 that the credit was somewhat higher than normal “because of
the particularly strenuous and difficult nature of the custody ... in this
case”. I do not know what evidence was before Hawco J., although I would
suspect it was not the testimony I heard about Ferguson’s treatment.

[
218
]

The
Crown argues that Chan’s treatment was not exceptionally harsh. The Crown says
that objective standards should be used and that it is wrong to compare the
approach of one remand centre versus another or to compare the federal
government’s correctional approach to that of the province. While conceding
that Chan was treated poorly in some circumstances, the Crown argues that these
were isolated incidents and that remand officials were trying to do their best
in difficult circumstances. Counsel for Chan counters that the commonality of
the mistreatment neither justifies nor alleviates its harsh consequences.

[
219
]

In
addition to harsh conditions, Counsel for Chan cites
R. v. Buggins
,

2002 ABQB 90
, to argue that in many cases the rate of statutory remission can
be refined, the submission being that Chan is likely to be released on parole
1/3 of the way through his sentence.

[
220
]

Other
cases on this point include
R. v. Whittaker
(2001), 301 A.R. 136,

2001 ABQB 873
, where Veit J. granted 3:1 credit;
R. v. Fujii

(2002), 323 A.R. 261,
2002 ABQB 805
, where Martin J. refused 3:1 credit,
R.
v. Jabbour
,
[2001] O.J. No. 3820
, where Watt J. gave more than double
credit, or what he called “enhanced credit”, for remand time; and a recent
Peace River case,
R. v. Thomas
, 26 July 2005, where Provincial
Court Judge McIntosh refused to grant more than 2:1 credit.

[
221
]

Another
issue to consider is the length of the detention. The Crown submits that Chan
has been in remand for a long period of time because he delayed the proceedings
of his trial and sentencing. He argues that if I award Chan an enhanced rate of
credit it will encourage other remand inmates to deliberately delay their
proceedings and to stay in remand as long as possible. Further, were Chan to be
released now, he would not obtain the benefit of the structured supervision
available to those serving federal time.

[
222
]

The
final credit issue is whether the period from 12 June 2003 to 29 October 2003
should count towards credit. The Crown’s submission is that, because Chan did
not apply for bail, the period up until 29 October 2003 should not be counted.

B.

Conclusion
on Pre-sentence Credit

[
223
]

I
am exercising my discretion and awarding Chan a credit of 3:1 for the period
from 12 June 2003 until today. Multiplying this total of 26 months
and one day by the factor of 3 yields the result of 78 months and 3 days’
credit. The reason for giving enhanced credit is the exceptionally hard time
that Chan experienced. The exceptionally hard time is detailed during the
review of the evidence and includes being repeatedly denied a vegetarian meal
that he requested for religious reasons. Additionally correction officers
applied force to him in relation to strip searches, forced him to wear a
baby-doll in disciplinary segregation and sent him on what remand officials
knew would be a long and difficult trip to Peace River after he requested a
second medical opinion. I am satisfied that Chan was able to demonstrate that
this treatment had significant impact on him. However, I am not convinced that
the applications of force have any connection to the post-traumatic stress
disorder described by Block.

[
224
]

On
the argument that Chan is likely to be released on parole less than halfway
through his sentence, I am giving it no credence because no cogent evidence was
introduced in this regard. Regardless of the evidentiary deficiency, I am not
confident that a Trial Judge can predict with any certainty when parole is
likely to be granted.

[
225
]

On
the issue of Chan’s length of time in remand, I make the following comments.
The length of the pre-disposition sentence has normally not been a factor in
increasing or decreasing the normal credit awarded. Two of the defendants in
R.
v. Tallman
(1989),
1989 ABCA 47 (CanLII)
, 48 C.C.C. (3d) 81 (Alta. C.A.), spent 20 to 21
months in pre-trial custody before finally being sentenced. Their lengthy
pre-trial custody was due to their trials and appeals being delayed by
Charter

arguments. The Court determined that the usual practice of credit was still
appropriate in this case. This same logic applies to this case. Given the
description I have heard about the conditions in remand, I am doubtful that
many defendants would want to delay their trials in hopes of earning extra
credit.

[
226
]

On
a related issue, I give no credence to the suggestion that Chan changed counsel
in order to delay proceedings. In

R. v. Mills

(1999), 133 C.C.C.
(3d) 451,
1999 BCCA 159
, the Crown argued that the defendant had delayed
proceedings because he changed counsel. The Court held at para. 35 that this
was not a reason to deny credit for pre-sentence custody, particularly because
solicitor-client privilege normally does not allow an inquiry into why counsel
was changed. A similar point was raised by Counsel for Chan.

[
227
]

Finally,
I am rejecting the submission that Chan should only receive credit from
29 October 2003, when bail was revoked on these charges, because he did
not apply for bail. I am counting the period from 12 June 2003 until 29 October
2003. In
Mills
, the Court stated that the accused likely thought
he would not get bail in view of his record. The same logic applies here.
Practically speaking, he was in custody since 12 June 2003 as a result of the
first charges.

V.        Conclusion

[
228
]

In
conclusion, I fix the sentence on Count 1 at 7½ years or 90 months’
imprisonment. This is reduced for the 26 months and 1 day spent in pre-sentence
custody multiplied by a factor of 3, which leaves Chan with 1 year or 12 months
less 3 days to serve. In addition, to meet the Crown’s concerns about lack of
supervision, Chan will enter into a probation order for 3 years on terms to be
determined. The sentence on Count 2 is one day concurrent. There is no victim
fine surcharge.
